He asserts that confidence in this bubble is what keeps construction going and warns that building more enlarges it rather than resolves underlying uncertainty about whether these facilities are even needed.

Monbiot criticizes the government's classification of datacentres as nationally significant infrastructure, which lets them bypass local planning control and go directly to ministers. He claims the ostensible purpose is growth but argues their real function is sustaining tech share values that could trigger collapse. He notes the government has admitted it does not know what these facilities will be used for, while listing some actual users he disapproves of: gambling and pornography operations, including child sexual abuse imagery whose reports reportedly rose 8,400% in two years; shitposters; fascists using algorithms to amplify content; and Russian cyber-attackers. He urges readers to accept the environmental costs—landscape destruction, blocked sunlight, light pollution, aquifer depletion, pollutants, energy consumption, and climate acceleration—and even job losses as necessary for national priority.

Monbiot warns that AI companies may be overvalued and datacentres possibly overbuilt, with only a few firms likely to succeed while others are left with expensive dead infrastructure. He argues governments should pause to observe how the sector develops rather than committing prematurely, since decommissioning costs could fall on the public if other failed industries are any guide. On policy front, he says Burnham's government is turbocharging datacentres to make the UK attractive to AI firms while continuing what he calls Keir Starmer's war against pleasant surroundings and good lives. He mentions a still-pushed regulating for growth bill that would create regulatory sandboxes where corporations can do things banned elsewhere, possibly including planned AI growth zones.

Monbiot also attacks efforts to remove the Aarhus convention costs cap—guaranteed by the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018—which could force objectors to pay life-changing or home-losing bills and shut down public participation. He cites a Spotlight on Corruption investigation finding that between July 2024 and June 2026, ministers met representatives from 137 businesses some multiple times, while meeting only two community groups and no environmental organizations. A submission by the Sovereign AI Leadership taskforce representing Nvidia, Microsoft, Cisco and similar firms reportedly warned of one year to force new datacentres through before public objections become overwhelming. He notes residents of Brick Lane discovered that even social housing—the prime minister's proclaimed defining purpose—is being displaced by these projects.

Monbiot concludes that while the government has classified climate activists and Palestine protesters as national security threats, he considers the genuine threat to lie in the highest offices of state rather than among ordinary citizens. He asserts this administration is as easily influenced by commercial interests as Starmer's was, describing an industry at odds with most people's aspirations for a decent life.

No visual element: the article contains no tables or figures worth charting; its key statistics are rhetorical claims and narrative points rather than comparable data series.
items.title: Monbiot: UK's datacentre push bets on an AI bubble

items.summary:
The Bank of England is undertaking a secretive, major renovation of its Grade I-listed headquarters on Threadneedle Street in the City of London. Governor Andrew Bailey oversees what his team describes as an "incredibly complex project" aimed at modernising the historic building while 3,500 staff remain working on site. The scheme seeks to preserve Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted ceilings while transforming parts of the neoclassical structure into a Google-like workplace with friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank plans for 1,400 staff currently based at its nearby office on 20 Moorgate to relocate to Threadneedle Street by summer 2028, while others take voluntary redundancy or move to a new outpost being refurbished in Leeds. Funding will come from an estimated £100m of annual savings over three years generated through 450 redundancies and other cost cuts.

Bailey's team is keen to avoid the delays and budget overruns that plagued the US Federal Reserve revamp, which grew from an initial $921m (£696m) in February 2020 to a projected final cost of nearly $2.5bn with completion pushed to December 2027. The Bank's project is smaller by comparison and pales against the possible £60bn Palace of Westminster renovation, though it resembles the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration that Bailey wants to avoid becoming another subject of parliamentary scrutiny.

The scheme was first announced in July 2025 with work due to start this month. The construction contract went only to Sir Robert McAlpine in October, a month later than planned. A Bank spokesperson said all procurement processes aim to deliver value for money and that there will be no delays following the appointment of architects last November.

Bailey's team is based in the Parlours and must weigh cost implications from new fire safety regulations, accessibility requirements, electrical testing, plumbing upgrades and renewable heating needs. Security concerns are significant: Bailey wants to ensure 400,000 bars of gold worth more than £200bn and £100m of bank notes in the vaults remain safe from terrorists and thieves during construction.

The fate of the Bank's museum presents a further complication. The public-facing museum on Bartholomew Lane currently receives about 100,000 visitors a year, mainly schoolchildren. Some senior staff wanted to relocate it into the central quad so visitors could enter through the main entrance, while others favoured cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern.

Vivienne Grafton, executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal that this is an opportunity "to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation." However, architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the City of London Corporation and Historic England. Anna Joynt, a senior architect at Allies and Morrison, noted it was common for preparatory works to begin before full listed building consent is granted.

There has been some tangible progress: the roof of the main portico is clad in scaffolding for repairs, and last year planning permission secured an overhaul of one small section known as the former governor's secretaries' offices. The rest of the 1.4-hectare (3.5-acre) site remains uncertain.

The Bank began in rented premises in 1694 before moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734, earning its nickname "the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street" from a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger. It was refashioned by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and remodelled again in the 1920s when much of the interior was demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which Gordon Brown gave independence to set interest rates in 1997. After the 2008 financial crash, it later received responsibility for regulating the banking sector under George Osborne.
items.title: Bank of England's £160m headquarters revamp faces cost fears

items.summary: A Japanese court in Utsunomiya, Tochigi Prefecture, on Thursday sentenced an 18-year-old high school boy to 18 months in prison suspended for four years. Presiding Judge Yumiko Takashima of the Utsunomiya District Court found him guilty under the employment security law for introducing hazardous work, and public prosecutors had sought the same 18-month sentence he received. According to the indictment, on May 13 the boy introduced a 16-year-old from Kawasaki in Kanagawa Prefecture to another 16-year-old from Sagamihara, knowing that the latter would serve as the perpetrator. The robbery-murder took place at the home of Eiko Tomiyama, 69, in Kaminokawa on May 14, when she was assaulted and died later that day. Four boys aged 16 to 17 are suspected of carrying out the robbery, while two others have been indicted as alleged on-site supervisors: Kaito Takemae, 29, and his wife Miyu, 25. Kazuhiko Masuda, 48, is identified as the alleged mastermind and remains wanted internationally on suspicion of robbery and murder.
items.title: Japanese high school student sentenced for introducing robbery-murder perpetrator

items.summary: Formula One drivers welcomed a signal from FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem that the sport is moving toward new power unit regulations, with some drivers expressing hope for a return to naturally aspirated V8 engines possibly as soon as 2030. Ben Sulayem indicated on social media this week that a shift away from current V6 hybrid turbo units was imminent, writing 'You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon…'. Formula One last used such engines between 2006 and 2013, and drivers noted the change could make cars lighter, simpler, and cheaper for manufacturers while restoring an engine roar many fans have missed in the current era. McLaren's Oscar Piastri responded to questions with 'Very,' before adding that he did not know whether the engines would match those from his youth but was glad the feedback had been heard, hoping the move would be more straightforward for fans and cheaper and simpler for manufacturers as a win-win scenario. Mercedes driver George Russell said the sound of the previous V8 era gave him goosebumps, describing it as 'the high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era,' while arguing Formula One should retain an electrical element to keep cars at the performance frontier; he cited wanting extra 400, 500, or 600 kilowatts of power alongside internal combustion to reach over 1,000 horsepower. Russell also cautioned that nostalgia for the final V8 years overlooked the fact that those cars were slower than today's machinery. Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli said returning to an older style would be cool and noted lighter cars as a key appeal, while two-time world champion Fernando Alonso stated he did not expect to still be racing by then, calling it frustrating that the change had not happened in 2014 after what he described as 16 or 17 lost years of pure racing.
items.title: F1 drivers welcome possible V8 engine return

items.summary: South Korea's exports surpassed US$1 trillion for 2025 on Thursday (Nov 19), making it the fourth country globally to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China. The trade ministry reported that this figure compares with last year's record of US$709 billion. According to the trade ministry, exports passed the mark amid a global boom in AI investment driving both export volumes and related investments. South Korea is home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. President Lee Jae Myung posted on X that now the achievement must be turned into sustainable growth by enhancing competitiveness of major industries and growing future engines such as AI and bio, adding that exports should improve people's lives through 'growth for all,' sharing opportunities with both large and small companies across regional areas. The Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won (US$121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to channel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education. Finance minister projections indicate economic growth quickening to the mid-3 per cent range this year on record chip exports, after expanding 1 per cent last year. However, domestic demand remains weak as export benefits have not yet reached many households; consumer sentiment has been weighed down by high interest rates and prices alongside unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market.
items.title: South Korea Becomes Fourth Country to Reach US$1 Trillion in Exports

items.summary: World Anteater Day falls on Nov. 19, marking recognition of tube-nosed, ant- and termite-eating animals across Central and South America that are closely related to sloths. The giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is the largest species and lives on the ground where it rips open anthills and termite nests with its razor-sharp claws and slurps up insects with its long, sticky tongue; the species is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Habitat destruction and hunting have pushed giant anteaters out of parts of their range, but restoration and rewilding efforts are helping them return in some former areas. In 2025, a giant anteater returned to Argentina's Alma Guaraní reserve in the Gran Chaco for the first known time since 1986, reported Mongabay contributor Sean Mowbray. Habitat degradation from agricultural expansion and forest loss had cut ant abundance by 30-50% compared with well-preserved areas, directly affecting the anteater. The Alma Guaraní Natural Reserve covers approximately 6,400 hectares (about 15,800 acres) and has hosted volunteer-led restoration for more than a decade; volunteers planted native trees in some spots while using fences to let other land regenerate naturally by excluding livestock, dogs, hunting, and fishing. A network of 20 camera traps found the anteater mostly stayed in passively restored areas, though experts caution it is too early to tell whether this return signals recovery or a one-off event and stress the need for continuous monitoring. Separately, in August 2023, Fábio Mazim's team captured footage of a giant anteater with its long snout and bushy tail at Brazil's Espinilho State Park; Mazim told contributor Sarah Brown that he shouted and cried upon seeing it and took days to grasp the importance of this record. Giant anteaters had not been seen alive in that region since 1890, and between August 2023 and February 2024 when Brown's story was published there were another 11 sightings; scientists say it is unclear whether these were the same individual but conclude it likely crossed over from Iberá Park in northeastern Argentina, where a rewilding project has released around 110 giant anteaters.
items.title: Giant anteater returns to restored habitats in Argentina and Brazil

items.summary:
China's Xi Jinping is set to host a historic summit in Shenzhen bringing together Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, and himself for what he views as an unprecedented diplomatic achievement. The article frames this gathering as evidence that China has moved from reacting to Western decisions made in Washington, London, and Brussels toward shaping the international order itself, with the futuristic setting of driverless cars, drones, and robots underscoring Beijing's economic prominence. Although ostensibly an Asia Pacific economic summit, Xi sees it as a demonstration of China's grip on global economy and politics.

The article identifies several pitfalls for Xi despite his ambitions. On Ukraine, now in its fifth year, China is reluctant to place the war on the agenda because doing so risks damaging European connections at a time when Beijing relies heavily on exports, while also wanting to avoid destabilizing Russia, a key ally. Beijing maintains neutrality by calling for negotiations and political settlement without condemning Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as the US under Biden and Europe accuse China of supplying components and buying Russian oil and gas.

On nuclear weapons, Trump has signaled he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting global stockpiles after New START expired in February. The last major treaty had capped US and Russian warheads; its lapse triggers fears of an arms race. Beijing resists inclusion, arguing its arsenal is considerably smaller than Washington's and Moscow's, so it would be unfair for China to accept their limits while retaining freedom to develop its own capabilities.

On optics, Xi wants tight control over the meeting through choreographed speeches and talking points, but faces two unpredictable leaders who have threatened to go off script. There is a risk they dominate proceedings and reduce Xi to host rather than architect, though unscripted moments could instead highlight his preferred image as a stable senior statesman amid Putin's and Trump's ongoing wars.

Finally, the summit offers little likely outcome but projects power ahead of next year's Communist Party Congress, where Xi is expected to secure a historic fourth term. The article notes China faces domestic challenges including a property crisis denting consumer confidence, heavily indebted local governments, slowed manufacturing, rising reliance on flexible jobs without pensions or social security, and one in five young people struggling to find work. A photo-op with Putin and Trump may provide Xi propaganda that his country's century of humiliation is over and that China now shapes the rules of a new era rather than merely being a rising power.
items.title: Xi's Shenzhen Summit With Putin and Trump: Triumphs and Pitfalls

items.summary: A Brisbane Supreme Court trial will be held into the death of 12-year-old Tiffani Scholten, who police allege was murdered by her mother Carrissa Kaye Scholten and long-term partner Aaron Paul Richardson. The pair faced Southport Magistrates Court on Thursday charged with one count each of murder as a domestic violence offence after being committed to trial by Magistrate Louisa Pink following a protracted homicide investigation that began in August 2024, when the girl was found unresponsive at their home on Bellagio Crescent in Coomera, Gold Coast. The court heard Tiffani had Rett syndrome, a rare neurological disorder causing growth issues, and weighed just 13 kilograms; her teacher Nicola Reid said she did not appear to deteriorate during 2021 and had a healthy appetite, though the diagnosis could not be confirmed. Justice Pink noted there was evidence that Tiffani had not received medical care for a prolonged period before her death. Ms Scholten's sister Cassandra Dunn told the court that Richardson's relationship with Carrissa Scholten was controlling and abusive, describing him as short-tempered and possessive, and said he had snapped in multiple phone calls and voicemails despite only one physical altercation between them. Dunn alleged Richardson was a cocaine dealer who kept drugs hidden behind a fake power point in the bedroom, that his drug associates were raided by police shortly before Tiffani's death on April 18, 2022, and that Carrissa Scholten had been too afraid to seek medical help for her daughter over fears it would expose Richardson. Dunn said Carrissa was scared of how Richardson would react if she took Tiffani to the hospital. Teacher aide Brenda Walker testified that Tiffani last attended school in December 2021 and missed 16 weeks during 2022, while Carrissa Scholten attempted to feed her on the night before her death. Both defendants declined to speak in court and were not required to enter a plea; their trial date has yet to be determined.
items.title: Mother and stepfather stand trial over alleged murder of 12-year-old girl

items.summary: Inox Solar Americas LLC has moved its 3 GW solar cell manufacturing plant in Greenville, North Carolina into the equipment installation phase while keeping the facility on schedule for commercial production in the second quarter of 2027. The factory spans 515,460 square feet and will supply domestic monocrystalline cells directly to company module assembly operations, producing Galaxion cell architecture alongside Gamma Series monofacial and Vega Series bifacial panels. The Greenville project builds on Inox Clean Energy's acquisition of Boviet Solar U.S. manufacturing assets, which included an established 3 GW module footprint paired with a planned cell expansion; by using existing infrastructure rather than starting from scratch, the company is avoiding greenfield timelines that have delayed domestic manufacturing efforts. This expansion addresses a structural mismatch in the U.S. solar supply chain: cumulative domestic module assembly capacity has surged past 75 GWdc to 80 GWdc, while operational cell manufacturing capacity sits lower at roughly 20 GWdc, with upstream wafer and polysilicon capacities lagging further behind at approximately 3 GWdc and 10 GWdc. Because of these gaps, domestic cell makers will continue relying on qualified non-Foreign Entity of Concern wafer imports in the near term. Bringing 3.0 GW of cell capacity online is designed to help utility-scale developers navigate federal procurement rules under updated Section 45X tax credit guidelines and trade provisions, which place pressure on project developers to prove non-restricted component origins to capture domestic-content bonus credits. To meet these requirements, the Greenville plant integrates automated inline testing, precision processing, and production-record traceability. Industry analysts note that transitioning a domestic cell fab from equipment installation to commercial output remains an operational test requiring cleanroom discipline and process engineering. Ashok Nair, President and CEO of Inox Solar Americas, said: "By bringing cell technology, module manufacturing, and quality control together within our manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with supply and bankability required for project pipelines."
items.title: Inox Solar Americas advances 3 GW U.S. solar cell facility to equipment installation phase

items.summary: Police revealed that a fourth Melbourne Cup, this time a replica, had been stolen during a series of break-ins at Melbourne racecourses over the Spring Racing Carnival. The thefts are alleged to be linked: thieves dressed as tradies took Makybe Diva's three consecutive Melbourne Cups, won in 2003, 2004 and 2005 and worth $3 million, from Flemington Racecourse on Monday, while the 1948 Caulfield Cup was allegedly swiped from Caulfield Racecourse during several break-ins between November 4 and November 11. It had initially been believed that only Makybe Diva's three cups were taken from Flemington, but police allege a cup was stolen four days earlier. The Victoria Racing Club has remained tight-lipped about whether it knew of the first robbery before Makybe Diva's cups were taken. Two men have now been charged over the heists: Sama Mirzaagha and Chrysovalandis Tassakos, both expected to face court again in February. At a hearing in Melbourne Magistrates' Court on Monday, Mr Mirzaagha was out on bail at the time and not present; his lawyers described the prosecution as rushed and called the brief flimsy with serious deficiencies, while prosecutor Jonathon McCarthy said the evidence included DNA, fingerprints and extensive CCTV footage. Further details of the alleged offending were not read out in court, and Magistrate Simon Zebrowski refused to publicly release a remand summary filed by police. Mr Mirzaagha's charges include burglary, theft and dealing with property suspected of being proceeds of crime; he is normally prescribed medication and requested to be seen by a nurse in custody, though his lawyers did not apply for bail at that time but said an application would follow. His co-accused, Mr Tassakos, was granted bail earlier on charges including burglary, theft, handling stolen goods, dealing with property suspected of proceeds of crime, obtaining financial advantage and obtaining property by deception; he is charged in relation to both alleged heists and was supported in court by his parents. Police had raided a Mount Waverley home as part of their hunt for the cups, which remain missing.
items.title: Fourth Melbourne Cup Stolen as Two Men Charged Over Linked Heists

items.summary: According to Mercom India's Q3 and Nine-Months 2026 Solar Open Access Market Report, India added a record 8.4 GW of open-access solar capacity during the first nine months of 2026, up 29% from the same period in 2025. Open-access solar lets commercial and industrial consumers procure electricity from off-site projects through the grid rather than relying solely on local distribution companies. Growth was driven by greater adoption of captive ownership models and long-term power purchase agreements, while a temporary exemption from Approved List of Models and Manufacturers List-II requirements for eligible open-access projects improved access to lower-cost solar modules and supported project economics. Capacity additions slowed in the third quarter, with 2.3 GW added versus 3.4 GW in the preceding quarter and down 8% from 2.5 GW a year earlier. Priya Sanjay, managing director of Mercom India, attributed this slowdown to rising module prices, supply constraints, grid connectivity delays, and regulatory uncertainty, while noting that open-access economics remain compelling but inconsistent policies and execution bottlenecks are limiting the market's full potential. Rajasthan led quarterly additions with 29% of installations, followed by Tamil Nadu and Gujarat; the five leading states accounted for 83% of third-quarter capacity. Cumulative installed open-access solar reached 39.3 GW by end-September 2026, with Karnataka holding a 21% share, Rajasthan at 16%, and Maharashtra at 15%.
items.title: India's record open-access solar additions in first nine months of 2026

items.summary: The Euronews program Europe Today reports that Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and US President Donald Trump are set to meet for a historic trilateral summit at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. According to Kremlin critic Bill Browder and Euronews' Russian edition editor Serguei Doubine, who provide analysis of the meeting's consequences, the three leaders are expected to discuss denuclearization and the Iran war, but not Ukraine. Following this summit, Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will travel to Berlin for a meeting of the 'Coalition of the Willing,' which is set to convene with senior officials from Ukraine along with its top European allies as well as NATO and EU representatives. The program obtains updates on these developments through Ignacy Niemczycki, Poland's Deputy Foreign Minister. Europe Today airs every weekday at 8 am, 9 am, and 10 am Brussels time across Euronews' TV channel, website, and digital platforms including YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram, presented by Stefan Grobe in a new format that runs for just 28 minutes covering the day's key events plus analysis of stories shaping the EU and beyond. The program is also available as a newsletter.
items.title: Europe Today: Xi, Trump and Putin trilateral meeting in Shenzhen

items.summary: Reuters reported that Bangladesh deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops on Wednesday as talks of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina returning to the country triggered clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks. The violence has been blamed on supporters of her banned Awami League party. On Saturday, Dhaka said it had completed the legal procedures required to secure Hasina's return from India, with the final decision on extraditing her resting with New Delhi. Hasina fled to India in August 2024 after having been in power for 16 years; her ouster came after several weeks of widespread student-led protests against her government. In November 2025 she was sentenced to death by Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal for crimes against humanity connected to a deadly crackdown on protesters in 2024. The former prime minister has reportedly requested a new passport and identity card from Dhaka, but the Bangladeshi government has so far rejected her request, prompting supporters of her party to take to the streets in protest. Last week the Awami League announced a week-long programme of demonstrations in support of Hasina's return, set to conclude with a nationwide strike on Thursday. Dozens of crude bomb blasts and torching of vehicles were recorded in at least 28 districts over the last 10 days; police data showed that at least 70 crude bomb explosions and 57 arson attacks on vehicles occurred between November 7 and November 17, per The Daily Star. Between November 1 and November 17, more than 520 persons were arrested for their alleged involvement in the unrest. On Tuesday a member of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party was killed allegedly by unidentified persons during a protest near Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, on the day marking one year since her death sentence. At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank were also targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since November 10; Reuters quoted the firm as saying this. The bank was founded by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who led the country's interim government after Hasina's ouster until February and has faced alleged hostility from her supporters. Dhaka has repeatedly demanded that Hasina be extradited and expressed concerns about the ousted leader being allowed to address her supporters from Delhi; the Indian government said it was for Hasina to decide whether she wants to return to Bangladesh.
items.title: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary amid unrest over Hasina's return

items.summary: On Thursday, 19 November 2026, while attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, President Donald Trump told Fox News that both the United States and China conduct espionage against one another. He stated, "We spy on China, they spy on us," and added his assessment that Washington is more effective at intelligence gathering than Beijing, saying, "I think we spy better than they do." When asked whether he would ask China to stop spying on the US, Trump suggested such a request was unlikely to succeed given America's own intelligence activities. He remarked, "They'll ask me to stop doing it, and I don't know if I'd do that." The remarks followed his planned unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit. Trump also stressed the importance of maintaining relations with Beijing, citing extensive bilateral economic ties between the two countries.
items.title: Trump Says US and China Spy on Each Other, Claims Washington Is More Effective

items.summary:
Prachi Saroop, a senior Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) officer serving as Principal Chief Commissioner of the Mumbai CGST Zone, has submitted her resignation. She filed a formal three-month notice to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman under Rule 43 of the CCS (Pension) Rules, 2012, citing personal reasons while thanking the government and her colleagues for their support. Saroop is among the senior-most officers in the department and had reportedly been viewed as a contender for a board seat.

According to The Secretariat, some staff members believe repeated setbacks in board selection may have influenced her decision. She was allegedly shortlisted and interviewed three times for a CBIC Member position but did not secure a seat on the board. Her request arrives ahead of another selection round for a CBIC Member that officials say is expected in the coming weeks.

Saroop holds a Master of Science degree and entered Group A service on September 16, 1991. She began as an Assistant Commissioner in the Chennai Central Excise Zone in May 1993 before handling central excise and customs assignments in Delhi. Her career progressed through Deputy Commissioner (2000) and Joint Commissioner (2002), including service at the Directorate General of Audit in Delhi and a deputation to the Department of Biotechnology as Deputy Secretary. Later postings covered service tax, central excise, customs, and vigilance work in Mumbai, where she served as Principal Commissioner in Mumbai Customs and Principal Additional Director General of Vigilance. She joined the Settlement Commission in Delhi in June 2023, became Chief Commissioner posted to Mumbai Customs Zone-III in August, and took charge as Principal Chief Commissioner of the Mumbai CGST Zone in April 2026.

Social media users reacted with speculation rather than factual statements. One user wrote that Saroop had been superseded by a junior for the Member post and claimed ego governs CBIC; another alleged she was taking time to enjoy her earnings before retirement; a third commented on how much she has earned. Officials countered that appointments follow a prescribed process and that seniority alone does not determine board membership.

The article is reported by Sounak Mukhopadhyay of LiveMint, whose bio describes his coverage across trending news, sports, entertainment, box office performance, digital culture, and cricket.
items.title: Senior IRS officer Prachi Saroop seeks voluntary retirement amid board selection speculation

items.summary: The Economic Times reports that LT Foods' share price rose 8% following its subsidiary's acquisition of US-based Maya Kaimal for $6 million. MK Food Holdings Inc., operating through its wholly owned subsidiary Maya Kaimal Foods LLC, markets premium Indian-inspired shelf-stable sauces, ready-to-eat curries and rice products under the Maya Kaimal brand, which it describes as a leading player among mainstream consumers in the premium Indian-inspired foods category. The company reported revenue of $17.9 million for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, up from $15.5 million in the corresponding period of 2025. In its regulatory filing, LT Foods stated that the acquisition is an important strategic step to strengthen its Ready-to-Eat (RTE), Ready-to-Cook (RTC) and Ready-to-Heat (RTH) portfolio, noting that Maya Kaimal's culinary and product-development capabilities will complement LT Foods' existing strengths while enabling broader products, deeper engagement with US consumers, and new distribution and cross-category growth opportunities. Management emphasized that the United States remains a strategically important growth market for LT Foods, with plans to leverage combined business strengths to create scale, widen distribution, and unlock meaningful cross-category opportunities. Ashwini Arora, MD and CEO of LT Foods, said bringing together Maya Kaimal's consumer proposition and innovation capabilities with LT Foods' scale, market reach and execution strengths offers a strong platform for sustainable growth and long-term value creation in one of the company's most important global markets. The article is written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or Investment Adviser and holds no financial interest in the companies mentioned as of publication.
items.title: LT Foods shares rise after Maya Kaimal acquisition

items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday listed a batch of petitions challenging India's marital rape exception for final hearing, fixing the matter for December 9 or 10 and aiming to hear it before the winter break that begins on December 21. The petitions raise whether a husband should be protected from prosecution when he forces his adult wife to have sex. This protection existed under Section 375 of the now-repealed Indian Penal Code and has been retained in Exception 2 to Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which states that sexual intercourse or acts by a man with his own wife is not rape if she is not under eighteen years of age. The petitions came before a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. Senior advocate Indira Jaising requested the December listing because the court was scheduled to hear a partly heard case at 2 pm; the Chief Justice said, "We will either have it on December 2-3 or on December 9-10," noting that finishing the part-heard matter made same-day consideration impossible. On September 9, the Centre told the bench that its earlier response in the main case could also be treated as a reply to the other petitions, and the court said it would examine whether prosecution could continue if the exception remained in force and whether the exception was constitutionally valid. The Supreme Court first sought the Centre's response on January 16, 2023, regarding the IPC provision protecting husbands from prosecution for forced sexual intercourse with adult wives, and later issued notice to the Centre over a similar petition challenging the corresponding Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provision. One of the petitions arose from the Delhi High Court's split verdict on May 11, 2022; Justices Rajiv Shakdher and C Hari Shankar agreed that substantial questions of law required Supreme Court intervention. Justice Shakdher favored striking down the marital rape exception as "unconstitutional," describing it as tragic if a married woman's call for justice went unheard after 162 years since the IPC was enacted, while Justice Shankar held the exception was not unconstitutional and rested on an intelligible difference. Separately, the Karnataka High Court had earlier ruled that exempting husbands from allegations of rape and unnatural sex with their wife contradicted Article 14's guarantee of equality before the law. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, came into effect on July 1, 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Evidence Act.
items.title: Supreme Court to Hear Marital Rape Exception Petitions in December

items.summary: Defence stocks including HAL, Bharat Dynamics and others rose up to 3% after Defence Secretary Singh said at the FICCI Annual General Meeting curtain-raiser that India's defence capital expenditure budget for FY27 was set at Rs 2.19 lakh crore. The ministry is seeking a further 20% capex hike, with officials citing the outlay's multiplier effect on the economy alongside higher contracts and stronger demand signals to industry. Singh said the ministry aims to sign another record value of contracts and remains confident it can meet its export target of Rs 50,000 crores at least one year in advance. India's defence exports reach around 80 countries across equipment from artillery guns to bulletproof jackets, reflecting growing maturity of the domestic industry; Singh added that fairly significant platform exports are expected. Separately, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said during a visit to Japan on Wednesday that India's defence sector is moving beyond self-reliance toward strengthening its global standing, with production and exports expanding at unprecedented speed as Army, Navy and Air Force capabilities grow alongside indigenous manufacturing. On the market side, defence stocks surged up to 50% in one month last year after military strikes against terrorist outfits under Operation Sindoor, before facing profit booking; strong capex plans supported them overall even during an earlier sharp selloff amid rising oil prices from a Middle East conflict. The Nifty India Defence index has gained 14.5% in 2026 so far and over 7% in one year, though it fell 3% in one week, 4% in one month and more than 11% in three months.
items.title: India defence stocks rise on record production and capex hike hopes

items.summary: Grand Theft Auto VI launched globally on Thursday (Nov 19), and Sensor Tower estimates that three-quarters of the roughly 17 million units sold are on PlayStation, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft. Analysts expect this to provide a major boost to Sony's PlayStation business worldwide, though not in its home market of Japan, where GTA is considered niche. In Tokyo, shares rose about 2.8 per cent versus flat trading for the benchmark index. Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda said current Japanese trends do not suit such games and that there is no need for them to sell well there; Nintendo's Switch 2 dominance and consumer preference for anime-style titles over realistic Western games are cited as factors. Consumer Sorataka Goto, shopping in Akihabara, noted the game was only on PS5 and Xbox with multiplayer online unavailable yet, saying she would consider buying it once PC support arrives. Elsewhere, Sony's movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day succeeded globally but faced competition from Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of Mermaid Island in Japan. Analysts expect GTA VI to soften the decline in PS5 hardware sales and support software growth; Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July to September quarter, down from 4 million a year earlier, which analysts attribute partly to demand ahead of the launch. Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote that he has modeled PlayStation profits materially ahead of Street expectations over the next couple of quarters on account of GTA VI. The release also bolsters Sony's slate after it delayed God of War Laufey by three months to May 2027. Separately, analysts expect procurement challenges as memory chip costs have risen sharply due to the AI boom; Yasuda said he does not sense Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware and that royalties will benefit the company enormously.
items.title: GTA VI Launch Boosts Sony Globally, Not in Japan

items.summary:
The Odisha Legislative Assembly was adjourned until 4 pm on Thursday after opposition parties disrupted proceedings. The Biju Janata Dal sought a debate on recent floods in Ganjam district, while the Congress raised the Kotia border dispute with Andhra Pradesh. Members of both parties displayed placards and shouted slogans during the disruption.

The disturbance began at Question Hour when the House assembled at 10.30 am. Opposition members entered the well of the House before Speaker Surama Padhy took her seat. When she allowed Parliamentary Affairs Minister Mukesh Mahaling to answer a question, opposition members raised slogans; some stood at the reporters' table while others shouted from below the Speaker's podium. Congress MLA Taraprasad Bahinipati was seen banging the podium during his anti-BJP protests.

The House conducted business for only seven minutes before the Speaker adjourned proceedings until 4 pm. BJD MLA Sarada Prasanna Jena told Press Trust of India that the party had submitted a motion to the Speaker a day before the session began, requesting a discussion on the flood issue after suspending all House business. He stated that when the Speaker did not act on their notice, there was no alternative but to demand a discussion themselves.
items.title: Odisha Assembly adjourned amid BJD and Congress disruptions over floods and border dispute

items.summary: The Indian Air Force showcased its air power and disaster-response capabilities on Thursday through a large-scale demonstration at Air Force Station Jamnagar as part of 'Sahayata Setu 2026', the annual joint Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief exercise held from November 17 to 19. The drill involved coordinated operations by the Army, Navy and Air Force alongside the Indian Coast Guard, national disaster management agencies, civil administrations, and representatives from friendly foreign countries. Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani emphasized that effective humanitarian response requires a whole-of-nation approach rather than action by any single agency, noting India's role as a dependable first responder in the Indian Ocean region and Indo-Pacific under its Neighbourhood First policy and MAHASAGAR vision. He cited Operation Dost in Turkiye and Operation Brahma in Myanmar as examples of past humanitarian assistance operations. The exercise focused on joint preparedness, clearly defined responsibilities, interoperability, and effective use of technology, with the goal of translating coordination into timely action. Participating aircraft included IAF Jaguar fighters, C-130J Super Hercules transport planes, Mi-17 helicopters, remotely piloted quadcopters for aerial reconnaissance, an Advanced Light Helicopter Mark IV operated by all three services, and the Indian Navy's Dornier aircraft alongside Army ALH and Cheetah helicopters. Demonstrations featured an Mi-17 V5 helicopter carrying a bucket to douse fires with firefighting robots support, another Mi-17 1B airlifting an Army vehicle, a Chinook heavy-lift helicopter transporting bridge components, and IAF Combat Free Fall Rapid Response Force personnel jumping from an AN-32 aircraft. The multinational AJHE-26 exercise aims to strengthen inter-agency synergy, operational interoperability, and international coordination in responding to cyclones, earthquakes, floods, and chemical emergencies.
items.title: IAF leads multi-agency HADR exercise in Gujarat

items.summary:
US President Donald Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The encounter was reported by Reuters as their first in-person meeting in more than a year. During the talks, Trump praised their long-standing relationship and friendship, telling Putin that he believed wonderful things could come out of it or at least start there.

The bilateral meeting set the stage for subsequent discussions with Chinese President Xi Jinping and a proposed trilateral summit involving all three leaders. According to Reuters' own quick-answers summary, this is described as a historic first trilateral meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia. Trump had earlier characterized the gathering as an opportunity to explore areas of cooperation among the major powers.

No official agenda has been announced for the proposed summit. Possible topics reportedly include nuclear arms control, the Iran war, global trade, and the Russia-Ukraine war. Additional subjects could cover supply-chain security, economic cooperation, artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, and technology governance. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters that Trump would discuss reducing nuclear weapons worldwide, which she said he considers very dangerous to proliferate.

On several sensitive issues, expectations remain uncertain. The US does not expect the meeting to produce an agreement, though Trump is expected to raise concerns about nuclear reduction and proliferation; China has been reluctant to join formal arms-control negotiations. White House officials indicated that Trump was not expected to raise the Russia-Ukraine war, although he suggested he might bring it up.

Separately speaking to Fox News, Trump said he would not seek help from Russia and China to end the Iran conflict. Earlier on Wednesday, Xi Jinping welcomed Trump at Shenzhen airport, marking the first time he had personally received a visiting leader there since becoming president; the two leaders shared a brief hug.

The summit also comes days after a controversy in which an alleged Chinese spy reportedly "honey trapped" former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, resulting in his departure from the company and tighter US controls on exporting advanced American semiconductors. The article's author is Prabhakar Jha, a digital news editor with nearly a decade of experience who joined LiveMint as a Digital Content Producer in 2026.
items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi to hold historic trilateral meeting in China

items.summary: Around 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuels, including ExxonMobil and TotalEnergies, have sent delegations to this year's global climate summit, COP31 in Turkey. This follows a pattern of heavy lobbyist presence at previous summits: more than 1,600 attended the talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan. The article argues that lobbyists slow the energy transition using what academics call "discourses of delay," spreading disinformation such as claims that fossil fuels are part of the solution or that future technologies will save us. Oil and gas companies reportedly increased their Google ads in the month before COP31, while researchers say lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy: pointing to lack of international action as an excuse for domestic inaction, and working to block progress at the talks themselves. A new UN report says it is now too late to hold global temperature rise to 1.5°C, with the world likely passing that threshold in 2030, partly due to lobbyist obstruction of policies targeting fossil fuels. At COP30, host country Brazil pushed back by launching an international partnership against climate disinformation alongside the UN and UNESCO; thirty countries have since signed onto a declaration condemning denialism and tactics undermining information integrity on climate change. Lobbyists gain access through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups as well as official government delegations, though this year's draft negotiating text references information integrity without establishing a clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel ties. Fossil fuels were only explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021 after more than a quarter century of talks focused on greenhouse gas emissions rather than their source. Petrostates such as Russia and Saudi Arabia have assisted corporate lobbyists, while Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates used their hosting roles to push new fossil fuel deals. At COP31, negotiators are discussing more than 100 agenda items opposed by lobbyists, including a UN initiative to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions. In addition to the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate "action" agenda organised around ten themes, some of which threaten fossil fuel interests such as transitioning to clean energy. Lobbyists are likely targeting calls to phase out coal, gas and oil, echoing last year's failed efforts by Brazil to formalise a transition roadmap, along with an electrification goal aiming to boost electricity's share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035, which could reduce demand for oil and gas. Australia is on the tightrope as Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen acts as negotiation president under a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey; domestically, the Albanese Labor government has accelerated its energy transition through battery subsidies installed in more than 600,000 households since last year and rapidly growing electric vehicle uptake, while internationally Australia remains one of the world's largest coal and gas exporters. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese faced criticism for omitting fossil fuels from his opening speech, minutes after UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels "go the way of the dinosaurs." As COP31 enters its final days with eyes on Australia and Turkey, progress depends on whether co-hosts secure agreement advancing Brazil's transition efforts; meanwhile momentum for moving away from oil, gas and coal is gathering outside UN talks through an April international conference and a growing Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. The article concludes that clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation remains well overdue.
items.title: Fossil fuel lobbyists target COP31 as Australia co-hosts talks

items.summary: Spanish government figures report that more than 11,000 migrants reached the Canary Islands in the first 15 days of November alone, a record number for any single period. This figure represents more than half of the entire tally recorded across all of 2025. The surge is intensifying pressure on reception facilities and emergency services as authorities struggle to manage the volume of arrivals. Regional authorities have repeatedly warned about insufficient capacity, with some smaller islands facing populations equalled or exceeded by migrant numbers. In response, Spain declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands on 10 November and allocated additional funds to expand capacity at state-run reception centres. A Red Cross spokesperson noted that most arrivals are from Senegal, Gambia, Mali, and Guinea, fleeing poverty and conflict in search of better lives in Europe. The islands remain a major entry point for migrants crossing the Atlantic Ocean in makeshift boats, predominantly from West and North Africa. The sharp rise in arrivals has become a prominent political issue ahead of Spain's 29 November general elections, with conservative politicians heavily criticising Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez over his government's immigration-friendly policies.
items.title: Record migrant arrivals strain Spain's Canary Islands

items.summary: Lyon marked its annual Beaujolais Nouveau release with a torchlit wine parade, as costumed revellers led wooden casks rolled down the city's streets or transported on tractors while trumpets blared. The festivities reached their peak at a staged theatrical uncorking of the season's first bottles, which triggered music, dancing and cheers as inaugural glasses were distributed to dense crowds. Beaujolais Nouveau originates from vineyards in the hills just north of Lyon and reaches shelves only weeks after harvest, sustaining what is described as a quintessential French autumn ritual. The wine is celebrated worldwide on the third Thursday of November, when it becomes legal at an exact stroke for producers to sell the new vintage; it is characterized as light and fruit-forward, intended for immediate enjoyment rather than long ageing. What began as a local harvest marker has evolved into a broad tribute to French winemaking heritage that brings producers and townspeople together in what organizers describe as an exuberant street festival.
items.title: Beaujolais Nouveau Release Celebrated in Lyon

items.summary: A dispute arose over MPP elections in AP's Nellimarla constituency on Thursday, centered on the allocation of two posts: Bhogapuram and Pusapatirega. The TDP leadership is reportedly prepared to allot both these MPP posts to the Jana Sena. However, the decision to give the Pusapatirega post to the Jana Sena has drawn resentment among certain TDP leaders, because former minister Pativada Narayanaswamy's son is contesting for that same post. The affected TDP leaders have expressed disappointment over being denied an opportunity for their family member in this matter. Separately, in the Achanta gram panchayat elections, sarpanch candidate Kodidela Satyanarayana released an election manifesto containing 10 promises aimed at village development, including a pledge to spend 50 per cent of his personal earnings on such development if elected.
items.title: TDP-Jana Sena Dispute Over MPP Posts in Nellimarla

items.summary: US President Donald Trump touted an "outstanding personal relationship" with Chinese President Xi Jinping during bilateral talks held Thursday, 19 November 2026, in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. Describing relations that began with his first state visit to China in 2017 and have grown "closer and closer" over nine years, Trump said he and Xi sat together for two hours during Wednesday evening's APEC welcome banquet and cultural performance to discuss key issues ahead of their formal session, adding that "I think something will come out." The leaders were expected to address trade issues, tariffs, and technology restrictions, including on chips. Reviewing economic ties, Trump pointed to the US-China Board of Trade established during his May visit to Beijing and the "30 for 30" tariff-relief proposal finalized during Xi's September state visit to Washington, under which each side agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of imports in a "very fair way." He said he would ask Beijing to expand agricultural purchases to meet China's "insatiable appetite." The meeting marked Trump's second visit to China this year and the third round of talks between the two leaders. In their last two summits, they agreed to "build a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity." Speaking for both leaders, Trump said Washington and Beijing want to help end the Russia-Ukraine war, noting that 25,000 people, "mostly soldiers" per month are being killed. Addressing the Iran situation, he said both nations share a strong interest in ensuring energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, stating "We both feel that very strongly on both points." Trump also highlighted counternarcotics as one area of potential cooperation, claiming seaborne fentanyl flows have fallen 97% following strict enforcement. The bilateral meeting followed Trump's talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and the three leaders were expected to hold trilateral discussions later Thursday; confirming that his earlier encounter with Putin served "just to set the stage," Trump predicted "maybe a successful" trilateral meeting. Earlier Thursday, Xi hosted the 33rd summit of APEC forum leaders. Fox News initially reported that the meeting lasted 13 minutes before removing its post, with subsequent reporting indicating talks ended at 2.35 pm local time (0635 GMT), lasting around one hour.
items.title: Trump and Xi Hold Bilateral Talks in Shenzhen Amid APEC Forum

items.summary: Sotheby's sold Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs, known as Chestnut Trees in Blossom, at auction in New York on Wednesday for a record $190.4 million (£144.8 million). The price shattered the artist's previous auction high of $117.2 million set in 2022 and exceeded its pre-sale estimate of $180 million (£136 million). Painted in 1890 during the final two months of Van Gogh's life, Sotheby's describes it as one of the most important works from that period to remain in private hands. The sale came after an eleventh-hour agreement resolved a dispute over the painting's Nazi-era history. Representatives for the heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the work may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis, writing to Sotheby's on their behalf and asserting it was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses suffered by the Fischer publishing company under the Nazis. In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs reached a mutually satisfactory resolution, with Sotheby's stating the work would be sold pursuant to their agreement. The buyer was not immediately identified, though the BBC had contacted Sotheby's for comment. The painting was offered as part of the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection. Its provenance traces back through several owners: Samuel Fischer acquired it in 1909 before his death in 1934; it passed to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936 after being deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933, followed by four further owners. The Blaquier family acquired the work in 1975 and held it for more than half a century before its sale.
items.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after Nazi-era provenance dispute resolved

items.summary:
The Indian government has broadened financial and logistical assistance available to exporters through amendments to four interventions under the Niryat Disha sub-scheme of the ₹25,060-crore Export Promotion Mission (EPM), made on November 17. The changes target three persistent challenges facing exporters: limited access to overseas markets, rising costs of meeting international quality standards, and high logistics expenses. The amendments are especially significant for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and first-time exporters that lack the financial resources and established networks available to larger firms, reflecting a shift toward extending support beyond traditional export clusters.

Under the Market Access Support (MAS) intervention, the maximum eligible export turnover threshold for airfare reimbursement was raised from ₹75 lakh to ₹50 crore. Micro and small exporters can now receive up to 95% of airfare costs for participating in international trade fairs, buyer-seller meets and trade delegations, while other eligible exporters may claim up to 80%. The mandatory membership period with Export Promotion Councils was also reduced from six months to three months. Officials note that the longer-term benefits will depend on whether participation translates into sustained buyer relationships and actual export orders.

The Trade Regulations, Accreditation and Compliance Enablement (TRACE) intervention expanded its coverage by increasing the number of certificates eligible for reimbursement from 462 to 600, addressing compliance costs associated with quality, safety, traceability and sustainability requirements in regulated markets. The largest geographical expansion came under the Logistics Interventions for Freight and Transport (LIFT) component, which extended low export-intensity district coverage from 13 to 34 states and Union Territories. LIFT also added Land Customs Stations and Integrated Check Posts among eligible port categories, incorporated waterways alongside existing road, rail and air transport modes, extended air freight assistance to Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and reduced the minimum distance eligibility requirement between origin and destination ports from 200 km to 100 km. The intervention will cover all exportable merchandise except items on a negative list.

The Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) president S C Ralhan welcomed the changes as addressing exporters' three critical requirements: access to international markets, affordability of quality certifications, and high logistics costs. He described the raised airfare threshold and enhanced 95% assistance for micro and small exporters as major enabling measures that reduce financial burdens, while wider geographical coverage could encourage new export hubs.

The EPM was approved by the Union Cabinet in November 2025 with an outlay of ₹25,060 crore for FY26-FY31. It operates through two sub-schemes: Niryat Protsahan, focused on trade finance, and Niryat Disha, addressing market access and non-financial export barriers. The article notes that the amendments' effectiveness will ultimately depend on timely reimbursements, ease of application, and awareness among smaller exporters, with the broader test being whether lower entry costs create a more geographically diversified export base supporting India's ambition to strengthen its position in international trade.
items.title: India widens export support and raises airfare subsidy to 95% for small exporters

items.summary:
The International Energy Agency's new World Energy Outlook 2026 examines how the largest oil supply shock on record could accelerate the shift toward electric vehicles and solar power. The article frames this as a key takeaway from the report, noting that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis persists, the stronger countries' incentives become to move cars off oil and generate more electricity domestically. Initially, the world had some protection: well-stocked inventories buffered the first shock while the IEA coordinated emergency reserve releases, Gulf crude took routes around the strait, Atlantic Basin exporters shipped additional volumes, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now consumers bear a larger share of the burden through higher prices and reduced consumption. IEA executive director Fatih Birol said that although the energy sector and global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper its effects will be.

The report observes EV sales rising in some countries affected by the crisis, alongside increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For nations heavily dependent on imported oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can reduce exposure to future fuel price spikes. Dave Jones of Ember described Hormuz as an event whose full impact is only just becoming clear, arguing it will speed up electrification and renewables faster than many expect, with much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 driven by the desire for cheaper and more secure energy. Solar leads renewable growth in every scenario the IEA models, nuclear power grows strongly, and energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push toward homegrown energy might play out differently across parts of Asia, where some oil- and gas-importing countries have abundant domestic coal they could burn longer.

The article notes electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand since 2019, outpacing global economic growth, driven by industrial motors, air conditioners, EVs, heat pumps, and data centers. Electricity approaches roughly 30% of the world's actual energy use by 2035 in each exploratory scenario.

On oil bypassing Hormuz, around 20 million barrels a day previously moved through the strait before the crisis. If shipping remains risky, new pipelines could route some barrels around it while buyers seek other suppliers or reduce consumption; under those conditions the IEA projects throughput falling to 8.5 million barrels a day by 2030 and below 2 million by 2035, with the Middle East still remaining the world's largest oil-exporting region. If the conflict resolves instead, oil and gas supply could rebound, while a delayed wave of liquefied natural gas might ease prices even as buyers refill inventories, and faster electrification could remove some demand from both markets.

The report also states that for the first time the world now uses more energy to cool buildings than to heat them. By 2035 the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third, with gradual rises in advanced economies, slowing growth in China, and faster increases led by India and Southeast Asia among emerging and developing economies.

On AI's energy footprint, under the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already hitting grid and supply chain constraints and facing local opposition in some places, while the agency flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

On climate outcomes, energy-related CO2 emissions stay near current levels under present policies, begin falling under stated policies, and drop further in the Additional Response Case examining stronger government responses to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require; the current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, with national pledges showing little sign countries are accelerating energy-sector emissions reductions.

The article also raises an immediate cost: although more people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, higher fuel prices and shortages threaten that progress, leaving around 720 million people without electricity and nearly 2 billion still relying on polluting fuels or technologies. The piece concludes with a promotional segment for EnergySage's solar installer matching service.
items.title: IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026 links Strait of Hormuz crisis to faster EV and solar adoption

items.summary: Crude oil prices steadied after an earlier weekly decline, as concerns over a return to oversupply and ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz largely canceled each other out. At the time of writing, Brent crude traded at $92.01 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $83.00 per barrel. Forecasters warn of an impending glut even though tanker tracking data shows flows out of the Persian Gulf remain below pre-war levels, despite a significant improvement from the war's early months. Vortexa reported that Iran has designated more than 50% of the tankers used by Gulf petrostates to move their oil through the Strait of Hormuz and on toward the Gulf of Oman and global markets. The analytics firm noted that these restrictions have not yet reduced the volume of oil moving through a shuttle relay system, with exporters adapting by adding an extra stage of ship-to-ship transfers. This has helped maintain steady outflows from the Persian Gulf, though risks persist as Iran issues daily reports of tankers striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz while attempting to move outside the channel Tehran has designated for free movement. Ing commodity strategists warned that further disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz remain an important upside risk, but rising OPEC+ output, resilient Russian exports, and building US inventories point toward a more comfortable supply picture. Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey added they expect the oil market to gradually rebalance, which would curb prices' potential for sustained upward movement. Additional downward pressure came from the U.S. Federal Reserve, which has signaled it may raise rates in December, weighing on demand growth and further limiting any upside for crude prices.
items.title: Oil Prices Steady as Hormuz Tanker Threats Offset Supply Glut Fears

items.summary:
Anthropic, the frontier AI firm behind the Claude chatbot, is floating on the US stock market in what has become history's largest initial public offering. The company raised a record sum of $107.3bn according to Sky News calculations; this figure includes another $26bn raised through a private sale of shares to tech firms. In a sign of strong investor demand, Anthropic increased the price at which it was selling its shares to $83 per share, up from an earlier guide of $70-$78. CEO Dario Amodei and fellow co-founders are expected to ring the Nasdaq opening bell at 9.30am New York time (2.30pm UK), after which the company will debut under the symbol "ANT".

The float arrives against a backdrop of market volatility, as tech stocks have fallen in recent weeks and pulled the Nasdaq Composite down by over 10% from its record high at the start of October amid Nvidia-related concerns. Anthropic itself remains loss-making: it posted an operating loss of over $8bn in 2025, with expenses of nearly $13bn outpacing revenues of $4.6bn. Revenues have accelerated in 2026, though the company faces the challenge of sustaining this growth and converting it into profits.

Garry White, chief investment commentator at Raymond James, described the IPO as a litmus test for market sentiment toward AI investing. He noted that a strong post-listing rally would signal markets remain convinced AI leaders can eventually generate sufficient profits to justify current spending on talent, infrastructure and computing power, whereas a weak reception or sharp decline could suggest investors are becoming more selective about converting rapid revenue growth into sustainable earnings.

In its prospectus, Anthropic devoted 90 pages of its SEC filing—around a quarter—to outlining risks. It warned that models may behave in unintended, misaligned or autonomous ways and cautioned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if not developed with appropriate safeguards.

Regulatory filings reviewed by Bloomberg News showed the lab sold just over 3.6 million shares to retail investors in the UK and close to 9.7 million shares to those in the European Union, Norway and Switzerland. Kathleen Brooks of XTB argued that Anthropic's trillion-dollar-plus valuation is more typical of a mature company with strong fundamentals than one it actually is; while revenue growth has been strong only in the short term, the firm remains unprofitable.

The share sale is expected to turn more than 4,000 staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. Anthropic's seven co-founders are all becoming paper billionaires through the deal: they are selling 23,648,646 shares worth $1.96bn out of the 980,000,000 Class A common shares being sold in the IPO, raising roughly $280m each for Dario and Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Chris Olah.

Pre-market trading showed strong enthusiasm. Derivatives from IG International pointed to a market value of $1.35 trillion in Hong Kong Thursday morning—implying more than 24% above the IPO price—with the company's fully diluted market value roughly $1.5tn. Perpetual futures on Hyperliquid traded at around $101, about a 20% premium.

Hargreaves Lansdown reported that 45,811 of its clients applied for Anthropic shares; the average application was worth £6,661 and customers aged between 45 and 54 were the biggest buyers. However, those clients had only been allocated 33.6% of what they hoped to purchase. Chris Beauchamp of IG reported that retail demand alone exceeded planned allocations by more than 60%, describing overall demand as solid from both retail and institutional investors.

Roger Lee of Cavendish noted the record IPO priced above the top of its range, valued Claude's creator at $1.5tn, was more than 7x oversubscribed, and saw shares up around 20% pre-market—helping Nasdaq futures trade almost 2% higher.

Separately, Nationwide Building Society said it had used AI "extensively" in onboarding customers amid a record first half of the year for current account openings. Pre-tax profits surged 38% over six months to September compared with the same period last year, boosted by lower costs and higher revenues including a 7% rise in net interest income. CEO Debbie Crosbie said more than 30% of accounts were still opened in person at its branches, which it has pledged to keep operating until at least 2030 despite job cuts following the Virgin Money takeover.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva told world leaders at the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen that AI was already boosting growth. She said this year marked the first with a material impact on global growth, providing a counterbalance to negative energy supply shocks from Middle East turbulence while also fuelling inflation by pushing up prices.

Georgieva noted rapid AI-led acceleration across about a dozen economies contributed to 3.1% global growth and 3.4% for APEC—better than feared but worse than needed—and warned leaders faced "a genuine urgency" to advance AI-related policies, including digital infrastructure, labour markets and risk mitigation around financial stability and cybersecurity.

The item also reported that Nationwide's CFO Muir Mathieson said cost reductions related predominantly to technology and third-party expenditure rather than job cuts, as the number of employees and people-related costs actually rose amid plans to hire 800 more staff for its own-branded business bank accounts launching next year. Georgieva added that countries risk losing out without digital infrastructure ready for AI and with measures to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.
items.title: Anthropic's record $107bn IPO floats on Nasdaq amid AI market uncertainty

items.summary:
Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company founded in 2021 by researchers who left OpenAI over concerns that it was not developing AI safely enough, raised more than $107 billion in its initial public offering on Wednesday. The sale of 956 million shares at $83 each exceeded the price range of $70 to $78 per share the company had targeted and far surpassed original plans. Its seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares, while additional private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia added another $26 billion in value. The offering valued Anthropic at around $1.5 trillion and made it the biggest IPO in history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion listing from June. Shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT later that day.

The company's rise has been rapid: its revenue jumped 1,300% to $16.3 billion in the first half of the year, and adjusted operating income reached $1.6 billion during the same period after a loss of $1.8 billion the prior year. Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, positioning itself as a primary competitor to OpenAI's ChatGPT.

The IPO arrives amid volatility for AI-linked tech stocks and concern about an AI bubble; Nasdaq has fallen more than 11% since early October. Analysts note the offering will test investor sentiment toward the broader AI trade. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, requested $5 billion worth of stock allotment, calling it one of the best ways to invest in AI applications.

Anthropic faces controversy over a conflict with the Pentagon regarding unrestricted military use of its models, which Amodei opposed for fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance. The company also flagged risks including loss of control over AI and potential political backlash ahead of midterm elections. Its prospectus nonetheless expressed optimism about AI's transformative impact on the global economy.

OpenAI had planned to list this year but postponed those plans likely into next year after an incident involving its agents hacking Hugging Face, though CEO Sam Altman promised a future public listing.
items.title: Anthropic's record-setting IPO

items.summary:
The International Energy Agency's World Oil Outlook projects that global crude oil demand will reach 106 million barrels per day (mb/d) over the next decade, with India showing the strongest growth at three percent per annum on average to 2035. According to the report, demand increases across nearly all sectors in emerging market and developing economies, led by India's three percent annual growth, followed by Africa at 2.8 percent and Southeast Asia at 1.4 percent. Oil remains the single largest energy source through 2050 as structural declines in China and advanced economies are more than offset by growth in these regions plus rising international aviation demand; the IEA also notes that real oil prices surpass $100 per barrel by 2050.

In its Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), India leads global oil demand growth, adding 1.3 mb/d to 2035, roughly half of the total increase in emerging market and developing economies. Global oil demand was 102 mb/d in 2025 and is expected to contract in 2026 due to an energy crisis stemming from conflict in the Middle East. Under a Climate Policy Scenario (CPS), global demand rises to 106 mb/d in 2035 and 114 mb/d in 2050.

The average annual increase of 0.4 mb/d through 2035 is primarily driven by growth in petrochemical feedstocks at 0.3 mb/d and aviation at 0.2 mb/d, while demand in most other sectors remains broadly flat or declines. Growth then picks up slightly to an average of 0.5 mb/d per year through 2050, mainly from the expansion of car fleets in emerging market and developing economies outside China, where stringent fuel economy policies are not yet in place and EV charging infrastructure remains limited.

Advanced economy oil demand declines by an average of 0.7 percent per year to 2035, with the European Union seeing the steepest drop as accelerating electric vehicle adoption drives fuel substitution in road transport; this decline is partly offset by growth in the United States from rising petrochemical feedstock requirements and continued mobility demand.

The IEA emphasizes that India's energy needs across sectors are growing fast and set to continue expanding rapidly. In all scenarios, India accounts for more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region worldwide. The agency notes India is adding over 12,000 cars to its roads every day through the decade, will see a 33 percent rise in built spaces, an additional 200 million air conditioners installed in homes, and surging production of iron, steel and cement; as a result, energy demand grows by 2.5 percent annually to 2035 in the STEPS, triple the global rate. India and Southeast Asia see the largest overall increase in energy needs, followed by Latin America, the Middle East and Africa.
